Cross-session MLP Velocity Decoder¶

Spike Band Power + Threshold Crossings → Index-Finger Velocity, scored on held-out sessions¶

Trains one MLP on many chronic Utah-array sessions at once, using joint SBP + TCR features, and scores it on sessions it never trained on.

Pipeline: raw NWB → normalise each session → PCA(5) fit on training sessions → window = 20 bins (400 ms), velocity at the current bin → MLP(128, 64) with velocity-weighted loss → R² on each held-out session.

Key question: frozen after the first 53 days, does the pooled nonlinear decoder still decode the sessions recorded 151–443 days after the first session, and does it beat a linear decoder given the same inputs and the same training rows?

Revised 2026-10-24 (EDA-08, EXP-002). The first version trained and scored the MLP on the same 30 sessions, so every number it reported was a training-set score (ERR-02). Every number below is rendered from results/exp002_mlp_heldout_v2.csv (decoder spec v2: velocity at bin t from features up to bin t, no look-ahead lag, D-18); none is typed by hand.

Dataset context¶

The data comes from a non-human primate (macaque) implanted with a 96-channel Utah array in motor cortex. The behaviour is index-finger flexion: index_position runs from 0 (extended) to 1 (flexed), and the decoder target is its velocity, index_velocity. Each session is one day of recordings. We have 30 sessions spanning Day 0 to Day 443, where Day 0 is the first recorded session (2020-01-27). It is not the implant day: LINK's recordings begin about 349 days after implant (Temmar et al. 2025, §3.1).

Why this data is hard:

  • No spike sorting. We use threshold crossings (TCR), a hardware-level count of how many times each electrode's voltage crosses a noise threshold per 20 ms bin, alongside spike-band power (SBP). Multiple units, noise and artefacts are mixed together per channel.
  • Electrodes drift over months: signal amplitudes change and some channels go silent. A decoder trained on early sessions reads a different signal a year later.
  • Velocity is 1D (index-finger flexion velocity).
  • The recordings are uneven in time: 17 sessions in the first 53 days, then a 98-day gap, then 13 sessions over the next year. That gap is the natural train/test boundary.

Splits¶

The experiment (scripts/exp002_mlp_heldout.py, EXP-002) fits every decoder three ways, with seeds 0, 1 and 2:

  • forward (the main result): train on the sessions up to 2020-03-20, test on every later session. The decoder is frozen after day 53 and never sees a later session, which is the only split a device could run.
  • grouped: five contiguous date groups of six sessions; each group is held out once and the other 24 sessions train. Sessions on both sides of the held-out stretch are in training, so this measures interpolation, not deployment.
  • in-sample: train and score all 30 sessions, the original notebook's protocol, kept only to measure how much it inflated the scores.

Each fit draws 20,000 rows from every training session, after the 300-bin warm-up. PCA, the velocity-weight threshold and every decoder see training sessions only. Two linear decoders are fit on the same rows: Ridge on the MLP's exact inputs (isolates the nonlinearity) and, on the forward split, Ridge with the package spec on SBP r_norm (96 channels, window 5).

Signal structure: PCA of the joint features¶

The 192 joint channels are compressed to 5 principal components before windowing. The diagnostics below use Day 0, which is a training session in every split.

In [6]:
"""PCA diagnostics — scree + neural state space (PC1 vs PC2)."""
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA as _PCA

joint_day0 = sessions_joint[0]
pca_full   = _PCA(n_components=30, random_state=42).fit(joint_day0)
pcs        = pca_full.transform(joint_day0)
evr        = pca_full.explained_variance_ratio_
cumevr     = np.cumsum(evr)
speed0     = np.abs(sessions_vel[0])

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
idx = rng.choice(len(pcs), size=min(8000, len(pcs)), replace=False)

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))
fig.suptitle("PCA diagnostics — Day 0 joint features (SBP + TCR)", fontsize=14)

# ── Scree ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ax1.bar(np.arange(1, 31), evr * 100, color="steelblue", alpha=0.7)
ax1.plot(np.arange(1, 31), cumevr * 100, color="black", lw=1.5,
         marker=".", markersize=4, label="cumulative")
ax1.axvline(5, color="red", lw=1.2, ls="--", label="n=5 (chosen)")
ax1.axhline(cumevr[4] * 100, color="red", lw=0.8, ls=":", alpha=0.6)
ax1.set_xlabel("Principal component", fontsize=12)
ax1.set_ylabel("Variance explained (%)", fontsize=12)
ax1.set_title("Scree plot", fontsize=12)
ax1.legend(fontsize=9)
ax1.set_xlim(0, 31)
ax1.set_ylim(0, None)

# ── PC1 vs PC2 coloured by speed — clip to 99th pct to remove outliers ───
p_lo, p_hi = 0.5, 99.5
x1_lim = np.percentile(pcs[:, 0], [p_lo, p_hi])
x2_lim = np.percentile(pcs[:, 1], [p_lo, p_hi])

sc = ax2.scatter(
    pcs[idx, 0], pcs[idx, 1],
    c=speed0[idx], cmap="plasma", s=3, alpha=0.5, rasterized=True,
)
plt.colorbar(sc, ax=ax2, label="Speed (|velocity|)")
ax2.set_xlim(x1_lim)
ax2.set_ylim(x2_lim)
ax2.set_xlabel("PC 1", fontsize=12)
ax2.set_ylabel("PC 2", fontsize=12)
ax2.set_title("Neural state space (PC1 vs PC2)\ncoloured by movement speed", fontsize=12)

Dimensionality reduction: why PCA?¶

The 192-channel joint feature space (96 SBP + 96 TCR) contains substantial per-channel noise and redundancy. PCA keeps the 5 directions of largest shared variance; components beyond ~8 each explain < 1 % of the Day-0 variance (scree plot). The PC1/PC2 state space shows no clean velocity gradient, consistent with chronic multi-unit recordings.

n = 5 was chosen in the first version of this notebook by comparing it with n = 8 on in-sample scores; it has not been re-validated on held-out sessions. In the experiment the PCA is refit on the training sessions of every split.

What threshold crossing data looks like¶

TCR (threshold crossings) counts how many times each electrode's voltage dips below −4.5 × RMS in each 20 ms bin — a fast, hardware-level spike detector. The array is (T, 96): same time axis as SBP, one count per channel per bin. Most bins are zero (sparse); active channels fire a handful of times per second.

Below: a 5-second window of raw TCR from Day 0, before normalization.

Model training (forward split, seed 0)¶

The decoder used for the figures is the forward-split fit with seed 0, refit here exactly as the experiment fit it: 5 PCA components stacked over a 20-bin (400 ms) history → 105 inputs per timestep, MLP(128, 64), high-velocity bins (top 25 % by magnitude in the training rows) weighted 4× in the loss, early stopping on 10 % of the training rows.

In [8]:
dec = fit_pooled_decoders(sessions_joint, sessions_vel, TRAIN_IDX, seed=0, sessions_sbp_norm=sessions_sbp_norm)
scores = score_pooled(dec, sessions_vel, list(range(N)), sessions_sbp_norm)

# The refit must reproduce the experiment's seed-0 forward rows.
ref = fwd[(fwd.seed == 0)].pivot(index="session", columns="decoder", values="r2").loc[session_dates]
for name in ref.columns:
    gap = np.max(np.abs(scores[name] - ref[name].to_numpy()))
    assert gap < 2e-3, f"{name}: refit differs from EXP-002 by {gap:.4f}"

print(f"MLP converged in {dec.mlp.n_iter_} iterations, {dec.fit_s['mlp']:.0f} s")
print(f"Early-stopping score (R² on 10 % of the training rows, not held out): {dec.mlp.best_validation_score_:.4f}")
print("Inference cost, multiply-accumulates per 20 ms bin:", dec.macs_per_bin)

Results¶

Forward split (the deployable question). Frozen after day 53, the MLP scores a mean R² of -0.152 (seeds -0.167 … -0.129) on the 13 sessions recorded on days 151–443. On the same sessions, trained in-sample (the original protocol), it scores +0.141: the first version of this notebook overstated it by 0.292 R² (seeds 0.258 … 0.311).

The MLP does not beat Ridge on the same inputs: MLP − Ridge is -0.153 (seeds -0.167 … -0.132). The nonlinearity adds nothing held out. Ridge on the same 105 inputs scores only +0.020 even in-sample, so the PCA(5) representation carries almost no linearly readable velocity signal; the MLP's in-sample score is fitted to the training sessions and does not transfer. Ridge with the package spec on SBP r_norm, trained on the same sessions and target bins, scores +0.003 (+0.002 … +0.004).

11–13 of the 13 held-out sessions score R² ≤ 0, depending on the seed; the best session averages +0.033 (20200811). The claim that one MLP "generalises across all 443 days" does not hold on sessions it did not train on.

Grouped split (interpolation). With sessions on both sides of each held-out stretch in training, the MLP scores +0.009 (+0.001 … +0.015) over all 30 sessions, against +0.004 for Ridge on the same inputs.

For scale: a Ridge decoder (package spec, acausal r_norm) trained and tested within one session scores a median held-out R² of 0.276 (scoreboard 58415f8, r_norm_acausal). Three seeds, no confidence interval: the seed range is the only spread reported.

Reading the decoded velocity waterfall¶

Each row is one held-out session of the forward split, from day 151 (bottom) to day 443 (top). The dotted gray line is the recorded index-finger velocity; the solid colored line is the MLP's prediction from neural activity, made by a decoder that never saw this session.

  • The window shown is the most movement-rich 800 bins of each session, and the prediction is rescaled per row (apply_gain) and smoothed for display. Even so, the predicted line stays close to flat: on sessions it never trained on, the decoder barely responds to the movements. The R² on the right of each row is computed on the raw prediction over the window shown; over the whole session (seed 0) the scores are day 151 -0.15, day 245 -0.25, day 320 -0.01, day 410 +0.03, day 443 -0.16.
  • The first version of this notebook read the same kind of figure, drawn on training sessions, as proof that timing is still decoded more than a year later; held out, that reading does not survive.
